strengths: PST addresses a relevant gap in multimodal NLP evaluation: gender stereotypes can depend on interactions between people depicted together. Testing both occupational associations and organizational power makes the evaluation useful beyond single-person demographic counts.

The occupational evaluation systematically covers 800 ordered prompts, including reversed left/right positions. Three human annotators per target and reported Fleiss’ kappa values of 0.88–0.92 support the consistency of perceived-gender annotations. The appendix provides occupation lists, prompt templates, annotation instructions, and detailed results.

The reported occupational SS increase from 10.00 in single-person generation to 47.38 under PST provides substantial descriptive evidence of a shift toward stereotype adherence in DALL·E 3. FairCritic’s lower scores are promising preliminary evidence that feedback can alter these associations.
weaknesses: The central claim of near-perfect fairness is not established by the metric. SS averages signed stereotype adherence, allowing opposing biases to cancel across occupations, even within the reported gender strata. Table 1 already illustrates cancellation: single-person occupational SS is 10 despite female/male scores of 50 and -30. FairCritic needs occupation-level distributions and measures of deviation from the stated parity target. Additionally, Figure 6’s 74.3% PST(Any) statistic cannot independently establish bias: independent, gender-balanced sampling would produce at least one stereotype-adhering person in 75% of pairs.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified for reproduction. Section 5.1 identifies the critic model and one-loop limit but omits complete critic instructions, images sampled per feedback call, how feedback is incorporated, and the final evaluation sampling protocol. Generation dates and handling of DALL·E 3 prompt rewriting are also unspecified. Promising code and data upon acceptance does not resolve these procedural gaps.

The claimed superiority over prompt interventions lacks a matched comparison. Table 2 evaluates occupational intervention on the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic across the full occupation set. Both methods should be evaluated on identical prompts with comparable generation budgets. An ablation using fixed critic-style advice would help establish the value of adaptive feedback.

Statistical support is inadequate for the occupation-level amplification and near-zero fairness claims. The single-person baseline uses only three images per identity, while the occupational paired experiment has one generation per ordered prompt. Confidence intervals and uncertainty-aware comparisons are absent. Differences in signed scores also conflate movement toward stereotypes with increases in absolute departure from gender parity.

Gender-label agreement does not establish correct occupation or power-role assignment. The evaluation lacks an independent check of role depiction, left/right compliance, and preservation of prompt meaning after mitigation. The annotation form permits 'Cannot Identify,' but its frequency and treatment in the binary metric are unspecified. These omissions leave task failures and exclusions as unresolved influences on the scores.

Reporting inconsistencies impede verification: Sections 3.2.2 and A.2.1 state 944 prompts, while the introduction and conclusion state 1,952. Under the stated balanced averaging, Table 1’s FairCritic power scores of 11.40 and -1.96 average to 4.72, not the reported 5.09; any different weighting needs explanation. Together with the metric and reproducibility gaps, these issues warrant substantive next-cycle revisions before a Findings recommendation.
